claim: PKA has been shown to stimulate mTORC1 by phosphorylating Raptor at Ser791 following β-adrenergic stimulation.
source: The canonical target of the glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor (GLP-1R), Protein Kinase A (PKA), has been shown to stimulate mechanistic Target of Rapamycin Complex 1 (mTORC1) by phosphorylating the mTOR-regulating protein Raptor at Ser791 following β-adrenergic stimulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work, as indicated by the context of the abstract referencing established knowledge.

claim: Liraglutide increases phosphorylation of S6 in CHO-GLP-1R cells.
source: Similar to Ex4 (Brown et al., 2018; Burmeister et al., 2017), liraglutide increases phosphorylation of the mTORC1 signaling target ribosomal protein S6 in CHO-GLP-1R cells, and this is blocked by the mTORC1 inhibitor rapamycin (Figure 1A; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and references prior work with Ex4.

claim: Rapamycin blocks liraglutide-induced phosphorylation of S6 in CHO-GLP-1R cells.
source: Similar to Ex4 (Brown et al., 2018; Burmeister et al., 2017), liraglutide increases phosphorylation of the mTORC1 signaling target ribosomal protein S6 in CHO-GLP-1R cells, and this is blocked by the mTORC1 inhibitor rapamycin (Figure 1A; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The PKA inhibitor H89 blocks S6 phosphorylation by liraglutide.
source: The PKA inhibitor H89 also blocks S6 phosphorylation by liraglutide or the adenylyl cyclase/PKA activator forskolin (Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: H89 has off-target effects including inhibiting the S6 kinase p70S6K.
source: However, H89 has some off-target effects including inhibiting the S6 kinase p70S6K (Davies et al., 2000), likely explaining why H89 inhibits S6 phosphorylation by insulin (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Davies et al., 2000.

claim: H89 inhibits S6 phosphorylation by insulin.
source: However, H89 has some off-target effects including inhibiting the S6 kinase p70S6K (Davies et al., 2000), likely explaining why H89 inhibits S6 phosphorylation by insulin (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: KT5720 is a PKA inhibitor with minimal off-target effects on p70S6K.
source: KT5720, a PKA inhibitor with minimal off-target effects on p70S6K (Davies et al., 2000), also reduces liraglutide- and forskolin-induced phosphorylation of S6 and the PKA target CREB in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 1C; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Davies et al., 2000.

claim: KT5720 reduces liraglutide-induced phosphorylation of S6 in a dose-dependent manner.
source: KT5720, a PKA inhibitor with minimal off-target effects on p70S6K (Davies et al., 2000), also reduces liraglutide- and forskolin-induced phosphorylation of S6 and the PKA target CREB in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 1C; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: KT5720 does not affect S6 phosphorylation by insulin.
source: Neither dose of KT5720 affected S6 phosphorylation by insulin (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The pan-Akt inhibitor MK-2206 does not affect stimulation of mTORC1 activity by liraglutide.
source: Two doses of the pan-Akt inhibitor MK-2206 that block insulin-stimulated Akt phosphorylation did not affect stimulation of mTORC1 activity by liraglutide (Figure 1D; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Liraglutide stimulates mTORC1 signaling in a PKA-dependent and Akt-independent manner.
source: These data suggest that liraglutide stimulates mTORC1 signaling in a PKA-dependent and Akt-independent manner.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data presented in Figure 1.

claim: The catalytic subunit of PKA directly phosphorylates Ser791 of Raptor.
source: The catalytic subunit of PKA directly phosphorylates Ser791 of Raptor (Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Liu et al., 2016.

claim: Liraglutide increases PKA motif phosphorylation on Myc-WT Raptor in a PKA-dependent manner.
source: Using an antibody against the PKA motif RRXS*/T*, immunoblotting of immunoprecipitated Myc-proteins shows that liraglutide and forskolin increase PKA motif phosphorylation on Myc-WT Raptor in a PKA-dependent manner (blocked by H89), but liraglutide fails to increase PKA motif phosphorylation on Myc-Ser791Ala Raptor (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Liraglutide fails to increase PKA motif phosphorylation on Myc-Ser791Ala Raptor.
source: Using an antibody against the PKA motif RRXS*/T*, immunoblotting of immunoprecipitated Myc-proteins shows that liraglutide and forskolin increase PKA motif phosphorylation on Myc-WT Raptor in a PKA-dependent manner (blocked by H89), but liraglutide fails to increase PKA motif phosphorylation on Myc-Ser791Ala Raptor (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Liraglutide-induced PKA motif phosphorylation of Raptor was observed in β-TC3 cells.
source: This was also observed in β-TC3 cells, an immortalized β-cell line endogenously expressing the GLP-1R (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: A high concentration of the Akt inhibitor MK-2206 (20 μM) did not affect liraglutide-induced PKA motif phosphorylation of Raptor in CHO-GLP-1R cells.
source: A high concentration of the Akt inhibitor MK-2206 (20 μM) did not affect liraglutide-induced PKA motif phosphorylation of Raptor in CHO-GLP-1R (Figure 2A and B) or β-TC3 (Figure 2C) cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Liraglutide stimulates PKA phosphorylation of Raptor at Ser791.
source: Thus, liraglutide stimulates PKA phosphorylation of Raptor at Ser791.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data presented in Figure 2.

claim: Liraglutide-induced weight loss was attenuated in CMV-Ser791Ala Raptor knock-in mice compared to WT mice.
source: WT and CMV-Ser791Ala Raptor knock-in mice lost weight in response to liraglutide treatment, but liraglutide-induced weight loss was attenuated in the CMV-Ser791Ala Raptor knock-in mice (Figure 3A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A–D.

claim: Liraglutide-treated CMV-Ser791Ala Raptor knock-in mice had a lesser reduction in fat mass compared to WT mice.
source: This was primarily due to a lesser reduction in fat mass in liraglutide-treated CMV-Ser791Ala Raptor knock-in compared to WT mice (Figure 3E–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E–F.

claim: There was no significant difference between genotypes in the ability of liraglutide to reduce lean mass.
source: There was no significant difference between genotypes in the ability of liraglutide to reduce lean (Figure 3G–H) or free fluid (not shown) mass.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G–H.

claim: Food intake was equally suppressed in WT and CMV-Ser791Ala Raptor knock-in mice during the first day of liraglutide treatment.
source: Metabolic cage experiments demonstrate that food intake was equally suppressed in WT and CMV-Ser791Ala Raptor knock-in mice during the first day of liraglutide treatment.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from metabolic cage experiments.

claim: Food intake returned to pre-liraglutide treatment levels in CMV-Ser791Ala Raptor knock-in mice by the second day of treatment.
source: However, food intake returned to pre-liraglutide treatment levels in CMV-Ser791Ala Raptor knock-in mice by the second day of treatment whereas they did not return to pre-liraglutide treatment levels in WT mice until the fifth day of dosing (Figure 3I–J).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3I–J.

claim: Energy expenditure decreased in response to liraglutide in both WT and CMV-Ser791Ala Raptor knock-in mice.
source: Energy expenditure (EE) decreased in response to liraglutide in both genotypes and remained significantly lower in CMV-Ser791Ala Raptor knock-in mice compared to their vehicle counterparts for up to 8 days of dosing (Figure 3K–L).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3K–L.

claim: Energy expenditure remained significantly lower in liraglutide-treated CMV-Ser791Ala Raptor knock-in mice compared to their vehicle counterparts for up to 8 days of dosing.
source: Energy expenditure (EE) decreased in response to liraglutide in both genotypes and remained significantly lower in CMV-Ser791Ala Raptor knock-in mice compared to their vehicle counterparts for up to 8 days of dosing (Figure 3K–L).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3K–L.

claim: In WT mice, energy expenditure only remained lower in liraglutide-treated mice for 3 days.
source: In WT mice, EE only remained lower in liraglutide-treated mice for 3 days (Figure 3K–L).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3K–L.

claim: Phosphorylation of Raptor at Ser791 is required for the full body weight-lowering effect of liraglutide via regulation of both food intake and energy expenditure.
source: These data suggest that phosphorylation of Raptor at Ser791 is required for the full body weight-lowering effect of liraglutide via regulation of both food intake and EE.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data presented in Figure 3.

claim: There was no difference between genotypes in fasting blood glucose prior to liraglutide treatment.
source: There was no difference between genotypes in fasting blood glucose prior to liraglutide treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Two weeks of liraglutide treatment lowered fasting glucose to similar degrees in both WT and CMV-Ser791Ala Raptor knock-in mice.
source: Two weeks of liraglutide treatment lowered fasting glucose to similar degrees in both genotypes, and there was no difference in fasting plasma insulin levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was no difference in fasting plasma insulin levels between WT and CMV-Ser791Ala Raptor knock-in mice after two weeks of liraglutide treatment.
source: Two weeks of liraglutide treatment lowered fasting glucose to similar degrees in both genotypes, and there was no difference in fasting plasma insulin levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Obese CMV-Ser791Ala mice were not significantly protected from weight loss induced by liraglutide.
source: Unlike lean mice, obese CMV-Ser791Ala mice were not significantly protected from weight loss induced by liraglutide (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A–D.

claim: CMV-Ser791Ala mice gained significantly more weight when fed the 60% HFD prior to liraglutide treatment compared to wild-type mice.
source: One caveat to interpreting these results is that CMV-Ser791Ala mice gained significantly more weight and fat mass when fed the 60% HFD prior to liraglutide treatment compared to wild-type mice (Figure 4C and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and E.

claim: Mice with higher baseline body weight tend to lose more weight in response to liraglutide.
source: We have anecdotally observed that mice with higher baseline body weight and fat mass tend to lose more weight in response to liraglutide. We now support this by showing a positive correlation between starting body weight and liraglutide-induced weight loss in both wild-type and CMV-Ser791Ala mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: There is a positive correlation between starting body weight and liraglutide-induced weight loss in both wild-type and CMV-Ser791Ala mice.
source: We now support this by showing a positive correlation between starting body weight and liraglutide-induced weight loss in both wild-type and CMV-Ser791Ala mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was no difference in liraglutide-induced weight loss between wild-type and CMV-Ser791Ala mice in mice with baseline body weights above 43.4 g.
source: There was no difference in liraglutide-induced weight loss between wild-type and CMV-Ser791Ala mice in mice with baseline body weights above 43.4 g (Figure 4I–J).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4I–J.

claim: In mice with baseline body weights below 43.4 g, there was a tendency for CMV-Ser791Ala mice to lose less body weight in response to liraglutide.
source: In mice with baseline body weights below 43.4 g, there was a tendency for CMV-Ser791Ala mice to lose less body weight in response to liraglutide (Figure 4K–L).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4K–L.

claim: PKA phosphorylation of Raptor may contribute to liraglutide-induced weight loss in obese mice below a certain threshold body weight.
source: These results suggest that PKA phosphorylation of Raptor may contribute to liraglutide-induced weight loss in obese mice below a certain threshold body weight.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data presented in Figure 4.

claim: CMV-Ser791Ala Raptor knock-in mice were not resistant to weight loss in response to setmelanotide.
source: As shown in Figure 5, CMV-Ser791Ala Raptor knock-in mice were not resistant to weight loss in response to setmelanotide.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Raptor phosphorylation at Ser791 by PKA contributes to the weight loss effect of GLP-1R agonists but not setmelanotide.
source: This suggests that Raptor phosphorylation at Ser791 by PKA contributes to the weight loss effect of GLP-1R agonists but not another Gαs-targeting pharmacological agent such as setmelanotide.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data presented in Figure 5.

claim: GLP-1R agonists reduce food intake and body weight and are approved for weight loss.
source: Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor (GLP-1R) agonists reduce food intake and body weight and are approved for weight loss (Drucker, 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Drucker, 2022.

claim: Exendin-4 stimulates mTORC1 signaling.
source: We have shown that the GLP-1R agonist Exendin-4 (Ex4) stimulates mechanistic Target of Rapamycin (mTOR) Complex-1 (mTORC1) signaling and that inhibition of mTORC1 signaling in the ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH) with rapamycin blocks the anorectic effect induced by Ex4 in this nucleus (Brown et al., 2018; Burmeister et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Brown et al., 2018 and Burmeister et al., 2017.

claim: Inhibition of mTORC1 signaling in the ventromedial hypothalamus with rapamycin blocks the anorectic effect induced by Exendin-4.
source: We have shown that the GLP-1R agonist Exendin-4 (Ex4) stimulates mechanistic Target of Rapamycin (mTOR) Complex-1 (mTORC1) signaling and that inhibition of mTORC1 signaling in the ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH) with rapamycin blocks the anorectic effect induced by Ex4 in this nucleus (Brown et al., 2018; Burmeister et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Brown et al., 2018 and Burmeister et al., 2017.

claim: mTOR is a Ser/Thr protein kinase that forms two complexes: mTORC1 and mTOR complex 2 (mTORC2).
source: mTOR is a Ser/Thr protein kinase that forms two complexes: mTORC1 and mTOR complex 2 (mTORC2; Saxton and Sabatini, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Saxton and Sabatini, 2017.

claim: The rapamycin-sensitive mTORC1 has unique accessory proteins including Raptor.
source: The rapamycin-sensitive mTORC1 has unique accessory proteins including Raptor (regulatory associated protein of mTOR).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about mTORC1 composition.

claim: mTORC1 activity is stimulated by growth factors, nutrients, and hormones by promoting PI3K/Akt-mediated phosphorylation of tuberous sclerosis complex 1/2 (TSC1/2).
source: mTORC1 activity is stimulated by growth factors, nutrients, and hormones by promoting PI3K/Akt-mediated phosphorylation of tuberous sclerosis complex 1/2 (TSC1/2) (Kim et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Kim et al., 2002.

claim: The GLP-1R is a Gαs-coupled receptor that signals via protein kinase A (PKA).
source: Activation of mTORC1 by GLP-1R agonists seemed unlikely since the GLP-1R is a Gαs-coupled receptor that signals via protein kinase A (PKA; Thorens, 1992).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Thorens, 1992.

claim: Activation of the Gαs-coupled β-adrenergic receptor stimulates mTORC1 via Raptor phosphorylation by PKA.
source: However, activation of the Gαs-coupled β-adrenergic receptor stimulates mTORC1 via Raptor phosphorylation by PKA (Liu et al., 2016), suggesting that GLP-1R activation can similarly stimulate mTORC1 via PKA phosphorylation of Raptor.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Liu et al., 2016.

claim: GLP-1R activation can stimulate mTORC1 via PKA phosphorylation of Raptor.
source: However, activation of the Gαs-coupled β-adrenergic receptor stimulates mTORC1 via Raptor phosphorylation by PKA (Liu et al., 2016), suggesting that GLP-1R activation can similarly stimulate mTORC1 via PKA phosphorylation of Raptor.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the citation to Liu et al., 2016 and the similarity between β-adrenergic receptor and GLP-1R signaling.

claim: GLP-1R activation induces mTORC1 signaling and Raptor phosphorylation in a PKA-dependent manner.
source: Here we demonstrate that GLP-1R activation induces mTORC1 signaling and Raptor phosphorylation in a PKA-dependent manner and show that this contributes to weight loss by the therapeutic GLP-1R agonist liraglutide.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: PKA-mediated phosphorylation of Raptor contributes to weight loss by liraglutide.
source: Here we demonstrate that GLP-1R activation induces mTORC1 signaling and Raptor phosphorylation in a PKA-dependent manner and show that this contributes to weight loss by the therapeutic GLP-1R agonist liraglutide.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: GLP-1R-stimulated mTORC1 signaling in the VMH reduces food intake.
source: GLP-1R-stimulated mTORC1 signaling in the VMH reduces food intake (Burmeister et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Burmeister et al., 2017.

claim: PKA phosphorylates Raptor at Ser791 in response to liraglutide and this is responsible for ~50% of liraglutide-induced weight loss.
source: We show that PKA phosphorylates the mTORC1-regulatory protein Raptor at Ser791 in response to liraglutide and that this is responsible for ~50% of liraglutide-induced weight loss.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: PKA is reported to either stimulate or inhibit mTORC1 activity.
source: PKA is reported to either stimulate (Liu et al., 2016) or inhibit (Jewell et al., 2019) mTORC1 activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Liu et al., 2016 and Jewell et al., 2019.

claim: Liu et al., 2016 show PKA-mediated stimulation of mTORC1 in cells incubated in serum-free media.
source: Similar to our study, (Liu et al., 2016) show PKA-mediated stimulation of mTORC1 in cells incubated in serum-free media.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Liu et al., 2016.

claim: Jewell et al., 2019 reported inhibition of mTORC1 in cells cultured in serum-supplemented media.
source: This contrasts with inhibition of mTORC1 in cells cultured in serum-supplemented media reported by Jewell et al., 2019.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Jewell et al., 2019.

claim: PKA exerts differential actions on mTORC1 depending on nutrient availability or cellular signaling and energy status.
source: Since mTORC1 is a cellular energy sensor, PKA exerts differential actions on mTORC1 depending on nutrient availability or cellular signaling and energy status, as originally shown by Scott and Lawrence, 1998 demonstrating that forskolin inhibits insulin-stimulated S6 phosphorylation and also subsequently shown by Liu and colleagues (Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Scott and Lawrence, 1998 and Liu et al., 2016.

claim: Forskolin inhibits insulin-stimulated S6 phosphorylation.
source: Since mTORC1 is a cellular energy sensor, PKA exerts differential actions on mTORC1 depending on nutrient availability or cellular signaling and energy status, as originally shown by Scott and Lawrence, 1998 demonstrating that forskolin inhibits insulin-stimulated S6 phosphorylation and also subsequently shown by Liu and colleagues (Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Scott and Lawrence, 1998.

claim: PKA phosphorylation of Raptor contributes to the weight loss effect of liraglutide in lean but not in obese mice.
source: In vivo results using novel PKA-resistant Raptor knockin mice suggest that PKA phosphorylation of Raptor contributes to the weight loss effect of liraglutide in lean but not in obese mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: CMV-Ser791Ala mice gained significantly more weight on the HFD compared to control mice.
source: Loss of PKA phosphorylation of Raptor in one or multiple tissues may contribute to our observation that CMV-Ser791Ala mice gained significantly more weight on the HFD compared to control mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Heavier mice tend to be more responsive to liraglutide.
source: This difference in starting body weight could explain why liraglutide-induced weight loss was not attenuated in obese CMV-Ser791Ala mice, as in lean mice, since heavier mice tend to be more responsive to liraglutide (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The brain is a key target for the weight-lowering effects of GLP-1R agonists.
source: The brain is a key target for the weight-lowering effects of GLP-1R agonists (Adams et al., 2018; Sisley et al., 2014; Varin et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Adams et al., 2018; Sisley et al., 2014; Varin et al., 2019.

claim: Regulation of energy balance by mTORC1 appears to be most critical in hypothalamic regions such as the arcuate (ARC), paraventricular hypothalamus (PVH), VMH, and suprachiasmatic nucleus.
source: Regulation of energy balance by mTORC1 appears to be most critical in hypothalamic regions such as the arcuate (ARC), paraventricular hypothalamus (PVH), VMH, and suprachiasmatic nucleus (Cota et al., 2006; Inhoff et al., 2010; Proulx et al., 2008), where the GLP-1R is highly expressed (Jensen et al., 2018; Cork et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cota et al., 2006; Inhoff et al., 2010; Proulx et al., 2008.

claim: The GLP-1R is highly expressed in the arcuate, paraventricular hypothalamus, VMH, and suprachiasmatic nucleus.
source: Regulation of energy balance by mTORC1 appears to be most critical in hypothalamic regions such as the arcuate (ARC), paraventricular hypothalamus (PVH), VMH, and suprachiasmatic nucleus (Cota et al., 2006; Inhoff et al., 2010; Proulx et al., 2008), where the GLP-1R is highly expressed (Jensen et al., 2018; Cork et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Jensen et al., 2018; Cork et al., 2015.

claim: The ARC mediates weight loss effects of liraglutide.
source: The ARC mediates weight loss effects of liraglutide (Secher et al., 2014) and is engaged by systemic liraglutide (Salinas et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Secher et al., 2014.

claim: The ARC is engaged by systemic liraglutide.
source: The ARC mediates weight loss effects of liraglutide (Secher et al., 2014) and is engaged by systemic liraglutide (Salinas et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Salinas et al., 2018.

claim: Hindbrain regions are engaged by systemic liraglutide and mediate its weight-lowering effects.
source: Hindbrain regions are also engaged by systemic liraglutide and mediate its weight-lowering effects (Salinas et al., 2018; Fortin et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Salinas et al., 2018; Fortin et al., 2020.

claim: Inhibition of PKA attenuates the anorectic effect of hindbrain-targeted Ex4 in rats.
source: Inhibition of PKA attenuates the anorectic effect of hindbrain-targeted Ex4 in rats (Hayes et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Hayes et al., 2011.

claim: The MC4R is a Gαs-coupled receptor.
source: Like the GLP-1R, the MC4R is also a Gαs-coupled receptor, and setmelanotide is approved for weight loss in individuals with monogenic obesity caused by mutations in pro-opiomelanocortin, proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 1, or leptin receptor deficiency and in individuals with Bardet-Biedl syndrome (Markham, 2021).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about MC4R.

claim: Setmelanotide is approved for weight loss in individuals with monogenic obesity caused by mutations in pro-opiomelanocortin, proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 1, or leptin receptor deficiency and in individuals with Bardet-Biedl syndrome.
source: Like the GLP-1R, the MC4R is also a Gαs-coupled receptor, and setmelanotide is approved for weight loss in individuals with monogenic obesity caused by mutations in pro-opiomelanocortin, proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 1, or leptin receptor deficiency and in individuals with Bardet-Biedl syndrome (Markham, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Markham, 2021.

claim: Liraglutide does not regulate mTORC1 via Akt.
source: Our results suggest that liraglutide does not regulate mTORC1 via Akt, as was observed for βAR signaling in adipocytes (Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript and contrasted with Liu et al., 2016.

claim: βAR signaling regulates mTORC1 via Akt in adipocytes.
source: Our results suggest that liraglutide does not regulate mTORC1 via Akt, as was observed for βAR signaling in adipocytes (Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Liu et al., 2016.

claim: Inhibition of Akt activity in the hindbrain attenuates the anorectic effect of Ex4.
source: Inhibition of Akt activity in the hindbrain (Rupprecht et al., 2013) or hypothalamus (Yang et al., 2017) attenuates the anorectic effect of Ex4, so identifying targets of Akt mediating the effects of GLP-1R agonists requires further study.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Rupprecht et al., 2013.

claim: Inhibition of Akt activity in the hypothalamus attenuates the anorectic effect of Ex4.
source: Inhibition of Akt activity in the hindbrain (Rupprecht et al., 2013) or hypothalamus (Yang et al., 2017) attenuates the anorectic effect of Ex4, so identifying targets of Akt mediating the effects of GLP-1R agonists requires further study.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Yang et al., 2017.

claim: GLP-1R agonists reduce food intake by inhibiting AMPK.
source: Studies from our lab and others show that GLP-1R agonists reduce food intake by inhibiting AMPK (Burmeister et al., 2017; Hayes et al., 2011; Burmeister et al., 2013; Sandoval et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Burmeister et al., 2017; Hayes et al., 2011; Burmeister et al., 2013; Sandoval et al., 2012.

claim: AMPK suppresses mTORC1 by phosphorylating TSC2.
source: Since AMPK suppresses mTORC1 by phosphorylating TSC2 (Inoki et al., 2003) or Raptor (Gwinn et al., 2008), GLP-1R activation could stimulate mTORC1 by reducing AMPK activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Inoki et al., 2003.

claim: AMPK suppresses mTORC1 by phosphorylating Raptor.
source: Since AMPK suppresses mTORC1 by phosphorylating TSC2 (Inoki et al., 2003) or Raptor (Gwinn et al., 2008), GLP-1R activation could stimulate mTORC1 by reducing AMPK activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Gwinn et al., 2008.

claim: GLP-1R activation could stimulate mTORC1 by reducing AMPK activity.
source: Since AMPK suppresses mTORC1 by phosphorylating TSC2 (Inoki et al., 2003) or Raptor (Gwinn et al., 2008), GLP-1R activation could stimulate mTORC1 by reducing AMPK activity.
evidence: The claim is speculative and inferred from the cited literature.

claim: AMPK can be inhibited by mTORC1 signaling.
source: AMPK can also be inhibited by mTORC1 signaling (Dagon et al., 2012), so GLP-1R-mediated inhibition of AMPK may be downstream of mTORC1.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Dagon et al., 2012.

claim: GLP-1R-mediated inhibition of AMPK may be downstream of mTORC1.
source: AMPK can also be inhibited by mTORC1 signaling (Dagon et al., 2012), so GLP-1R-mediated inhibition of AMPK may be downstream of mTORC1.
evidence: The claim is speculative and inferred from the cited literature.

claim: PKA-mediated phosphorylation of Raptor and increased mTORC1 signaling contributes to the weight-lowering effect of liraglutide.
source: In summary, we have uncovered a novel signaling mechanism downstream of the GLP-1R characterized by PKA-mediated phosphorylation of Raptor and increased mTORC1 signaling that contributes to the weight-lowering effect of liraglutide.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: GLP-1R agonists continue to be used as glucose-lowering agents for type 2 diabetes based on their insulinotropic effect via pancreatic β-cells.
source: GLP-1R agonists continue to be used as glucose-lowering agents for type 2 diabetes based on their insulinotropic effect via pancreatic β-cells (Drucker, 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Drucker, 2022.

claim: The PKA-mTORC1 interaction could contribute to the insulinotropic effect or another β-cell phenotype associated with GLP-1R agonists.
source: The PKA-mTORC1 interaction could contribute to this or another β-cell phenotype associated with GLP-1R agonists (e.g. proliferation/cytoprotection).
evidence: The claim is speculative about potential mechanisms.

claim: GLP-1R agonists display cardioprotective effects.
source: Furthermore, GLP-1R agonists also display cardioprotective effects that could be mediated directly via effects on the heart and vasculature and/or be secondary to the ability of these drugs to improve glycemia, body weight, lipid profiles, and inflammation (Ussher and Drucker, 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Ussher and Drucker, 2023.
